public_rationale: The condition held. Oil kept rising after the March 10 post, and EIA puts the monthly Brent peak at about $117 in April 2026. Jet fuel also 'escalated alarmingly' in March and April, per TAC Index. Air freight then became unusually expensive. By June 1 the global Baltic Air Freight Index was about 33% above a year earlier, at levels usually seen only in peak season. TAC also reported very significant year-on-year gains on Taiwan to US routes. That fits his example of flying GB200 racks from Taiwan to Texas. The other example, the cost of mobilizing the Abilene workforce, has no public data and is not scored.
limitations: Only the air freight example could be checked; the Abilene workforce cost part is unverified.
'Extra-normally' has no threshold; I read it as well above normal year-on-year moves.
Freight rates also rose on AI cargo demand, not only on fuel.
Oil dipped in June before rising again in September.

from_speaker: As the price of oil continues to skyrocket
flying a Boeing 747 filled with GB200 racks from Taiwan to Texas
mobilizing the thousands of people that work ... to build Stargate Abilene
our_interpretation: Condition: oil prices keep rising sharply after the post.
Plain reading of 'extra-normally more expensive': unusually large cost increases, well beyond normal year-to-year changes.
The air freight example can be checked with published air cargo indices for Asia and Taiwan to US lanes. The cost of mobilizing the Abilene workforce has no public measure.
I read the two examples as illustrations of one forecast, so the freight example can settle it if the Abilene costs cannot be measured.
criteria.support_condition: Oil keeps rising after the post, and air freight rates from Taiwan or Asia to the US rise unusually (well above normal year-on-year moves), or Abilene construction mobilization costs are shown to rise unusually.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Oil keeps rising, but air freight rates from Asia to the US stay normal or fall, and no unusual rise in Abilene mobilization costs appears.

evidence.excerpt: The Brent crude oil spot price averaged $85 per barrel (b) in June, down $22/b from May and $32/b from the April 2026 peak.
evidence.explanation: Oil kept climbing after the March 10 post, to a monthly peak of about $117 in April 2026, before easing in June.

evidence.excerpt: jet fuel prices, which had escalated alarmingly over the previous two months after the start of the US/Israel war with Iran.
evidence.explanation: Jet fuel, the fuel that matters for flying racks, kept rising sharply through March and April 2026.

evidence.excerpt: leaving it up some +32.7% from 12 months earlier, which is still above levels only seen in recent years at the height of peak season.
evidence.explanation: Global air freight rates were about a third higher than a year earlier, at levels normally seen only in peak season. That is an unusual rise.

evidence.excerpt: the TAC air freight pricing data, which continue to show very significant gains YoY both to Europe and the US.
evidence.locator: paragraph near end, on South Korea and Taiwan
evidence.explanation: Air freight from Taiwan to the US, the route he named, showed very large year-on-year rate gains.

conclusive_event.meets_rule: While oil and jet fuel were rising after the post, the global air freight index stood about 33% above a year earlier at peak-season levels, and Taiwan to US lanes showed very significant gains.
